🧵

The Wyvern Fellowship calls itself a “Not for profit NGO supporting British communities”. Its own words, on its own platforms, tell a fuller story...

On 28 September, The Podcast of the Lotus Eaters ran a segment promoting a new organisation called The Wyvern Fellowship. The channel has more than 600,000 subscribers on YouTube. The three regular hosts, Luca Johnson, Harry Robinson and Firas Modad, presented it as a practical, British-focused mutual-aid and heritage network.

No one from the Fellowship appeared. The presenter told viewers he didn’t know anyone inside the organisation professionally, and that it didn’t know he was making the segment. Near the end, one host asked who actually runs it. None of the panel knew. After a pause, in which the hosts appeared to be listening to someone off air, they laughed, and one remarked that a guy in the chat apparently runs it.

It was an odd gap in a segment urging viewers to sign up and pay. The answer takes one quick search of Companies House. The Fellowship’s own website is less forthcoming. Its mission page refers to a “small board of directors” without naming anyone, and the founder’s name appears only as the byline on the Journal’s opinion essays.

The Fellowship thanked the hosts for “such a stellar promotion” on both @X and @facebook, and pinned the post to the top of its X profile. Directly above it, the X bio describes the Fellowship in eight words: “Not for profit NGO supporting British communities.”

“Not for profit NGO supporting British communities” is a reassuring phrase, built from the vocabulary of civil society. Each word holds up less well on inspection.

“Not for profit”

The Wyvern Fellowship Ltd (company number 17438355) was incorporated on 4 September 2026 as a private company limited by guarantee. Its incorporation documents name a single subscriber, Joseph Francis Mason. He is:

- the sole director;

- the company secretary;

- the only person with significant control, holding 75% or more of the voting rights and the right to appoint or remove the board;

- the company’s only guarantor, liable for £1 if it is wound up. A £1 guarantee is normal for this kind of company. What matters is who holds it.

During the segment on Lotus Eaters, a host told viewers that it is “the members that are the guarantors”. The Fellowship’s own terms say otherwise. Paying Fellows get no right to vote at, attend or take part in a general meeting, and none of the other rights of a company member. That applies at every level, from £2.99 a month to the £1,499.99-a-year Patron tier. Under the Fellowship’s Articles, those rights belong only to the directors, and there is currently one.

The directors also have “absolute discretion” over who becomes a Fellow, and can remove anyone for any reason they consider appropriate. Future directors are to be drawn mainly from “National Fellows”, whom the directors themselves select on grounds that include “character”. The mission page’s “small board of directors” is, at present, one man.

None of this is unlawful, or unusual for a company only weeks old. But it matters for how much weight “not for profit” can bear, for three reasons.

1. It is lightly regulated.

The Fellowship is candid that it is not a registered charity and that donations attract no Gift Aid, and it deserves credit for saying so. But the choice of structure has consequences. A charity answers to the Charity Commission, files a trustees’ report, and has trustees legally bound to act in its interests. A community interest company has a statutory asset lock and its own regulator. A company limited by guarantee has neither.

2. The promises sit in documents one person controls. 

The Fellowship says its Articles contain an asset lock: income spent only on its objects, nothing distributed to members, and any remaining assets passed to a similar body on winding up. As the company’s only member, its director could in principle amend the Articles, unless those clauses are specially entrenched.

3. No accounts are due for a long time.

The first accounts are not due until 4 June 2028, covering the period to 30 September 2027. In the meantime the Fellowship is collecting subscriptions, donations, gift memberships and Patron fees. For the next twenty months, supporters have to take “not for profit” on trust.

“NGO”

NGO stands for non-governmental organisation, but you may not know that in the UK it has no legal meaning. There is no register and no regulator. Any independent not-for-profit body can call itself one, whatever its legal form. What the label adds is borrowed legitimacy: the language of Oxfam and Amnesty, of civil society and good works.

The Fellowship takes that form while casting established charities as the enemy.

On the podcast, the presenter said mainstream charities had ended up siding “with the illegal invasion of Britain against us”. He compared the Fellowship to Martin Sellner’s attempt to build “a really robust NGO” on the continent.

Sellner, a leader of Austria’s identitarian movement, promotes “remigration”, which Julia Ebner of the Institute for Strategic Dialogue describes as a euphemism for the mass deportation of Europeans with migrant backgrounds. At a meeting near Potsdam in November 2023, attended by members of Germany’s AfD, he presented a remigration plan that extended to “unassimilated citizens”, according to the investigative outlet Correctiv.

The Fellowship’s own Facebook page goes further. On 20 September it wrote: “When the @RNLI assists criminals breaking into our country, we know they are working against us.” It shared a graphic urging followers to “follow the money” on the lifeboat charity’s funding. The Fellowship’s own first accounts are not due until 2028.

To outsiders, the label signals respectability. To insiders, it signals a counter-institution. In Theo van Leeuwen’s terms, this is legitimation by authorisation: the authority comes from the institutional form itself, before anyone asks what the institution does.

“Supporting”

The present tense does a lot of work here.

The flagship project, First Ticket, offers young people who left school with few qualifications accredited safety training for building sites, help with a site card and introductions to employers. That is a genuinely useful idea in a country short of skilled trades. But as of mid-October, applications had not opened and the training provider had not been named.

The podcast called the courses free, and so does the Fellowship’s Facebook page. Its own Journal announcement says participants must become Fellows, which means a paid subscription. It does offer to help anyone who cannot afford the entry tier.

The employers waiting for First Ticket graduates are part of a stated plan. On 19 September, the Fellowship said its mission was to connect “as many pro-British business owners as possible”, so that young people could find jobs “where they won’t be ‘cancelled’ over politics”. That describes a politically filtered employment network.

The mutual aid the hosts praised at length is listed on the membership page as “in development”. Mutual-aid schemes, local chapter activities and apprenticeships are not included in any tier.

The research page promises publications that are coming soon.

Its Almanac has so far published one practical guide, on investigating housing associations through public records. It is careful and lawful, and it warns readers repeatedly that red flags are not proof of wrongdoing.

Even the company’s own registration describes its business as research, education and running a membership organisation.

What a supporter can buy today is membership: members-only Journal essays, a Discord server, newsletters, eventually a Wyvern pin, and for Patrons a “Round Table” and an annual dinner. The bio presents an aspiration as a fact.

“British communities”

Arguably, this is the most important phrase in the bio, and the least defined. “Communities”, in the plural, suggests places: towns, estates, neighbourhoods. The Fellowship describes itself differently depending on where it is speaking.

On X, it is a “Not for profit NGO supporting British communities”.

On Facebook, it is “dedicated to uniting patriots across Britain”.

On its website, “national membership is open to all”, and its FAQ says Fellowship is open to anyone who wants to join.

On 9 September, its Facebook page listed the numbers of Muslim, Jewish, Hindu and Sikh charities in the UK, and claimed there are “over 9,000” Black and minority ethnic charities and community groups.

It then asked how many advocacy groups exist for the English, Scots, Welsh and Northern Irish: “Zero. Until now. Join the Wyvern Fellowship, Britain’s first NGO led by and for the British.”

That comparison is misleading in at least three ways.

1. It leaves out Christian charities, by far the largest group of faith charities. In 2016, New Philanthropy Capital found that nearly two-thirds of Britain’s faith-based charities, more than 32,000, were Christian.

2. It treats mosques, synagogues and gurdwaras registered as charities as though they were ethnic lobbying groups.

3. “Zero” ignores bodies such as the Royal Society of St George, founded in 1894 to promote English patriotism, which holds a Royal Charter and counts the King as its patron.

It also sets religious minorities on one side and the nations of Britain on the other, as if they were separate groups.

An association restricted to people of a shared national or ethnic origin is not necessarily unlawful. Equality law allows it, except where the restriction is by colour. But “open to all” and “led by and for the British” cannot both describe the same organisation.

Other texts point the same way. The First Ticket announcement describes the Fellowship as a network of people who “look after their own”.

The Journal’s “Setting the Record Straight” series, all bylined Joe Mason, has run at about one essay a week since 6 September. The full essays are for paying members only. This article quotes only what the Fellowship has published openly:

- Issue 2, “Who are the British?”, opens: “This land is our birthright”.

- Issue 3 promises to prove “how deeply wrong” the idea of “White privilege” is.

- Issue 4, “Two-Tier Injustice”, says Britain is living “under a hostile force of occupation”, with “the nations of Britain… held hostage to an utterly corrupt and decadent ‘YooKay’ Empire”.

“Yookay” is a term from the online right. The New Statesman’s Nicholas Harris traces it to 4chan and describes it as shorthand for a Britain supposedly overrun by immigrants and disorder, illustrated by what he calls “a racialised and frequently racist scrapbook” of images.

The words of the teaser leave the occupier unnamed, or point at the state. The image chosen to illustrate it, a crowd of masked men in black at a protest, one carrying a Palestinian flag, fits the scrapbook Harris describes. The text says one thing and the picture another, so the Fellowship can deny the harder reading while still conveying it.

- Issue 6, “The Indigenous English”, promoted on 5 October, rejects Jacob Rees-Mogg’s claim, made on 22 September, that the English are “a mongrel people”. 

Rees-Mogg had argued that Englishness is a matter of values and culture, and dismissed the idea that DNA makes anyone English. The Fellowship’s reply argues the opposite: “English genetic continuity is real and far sturdier in comparison with the layered histories of many African and Asian populations”. The promotional post summed it up: “The English are real, and are indigenous.” Silver Fellows could read it at once, and Bronze Fellows had to wait four days.

Both readings of “British communities” can be held at once, and that is what makes the phrase work. Prof Ruth Wodak calls this calculated ambivalence: a message built so that different audiences hear different things, and the speaker can deny the harder reading. A newcomer on X hears “local communities”. A follower on Facebook hears “patriots”, and “led by and for the British”. Van Dijk’s ideological square helps explain how “our own” operates. It foregrounds the virtues of an in-group without ever having to define it, and lets the out-group define it by contrast.

The Fellowship’s posts and words on X and Facebook are less guarded than its website.

Invasive species.

On 24 September the Fellowship’s Facebook page posted that “native wildlife is being pushed out just like native people”, listing grey squirrels, American mink and Japanese knotweed. It concluded: “A landscape full of the wrong species is not a healthy one. Protecting Britain means defending what belongs here.” Comparing people to invasive species is one of the oldest dehumanising metaphors in anti-immigrant discourse.

The day before, the Fellowship had accused “public figures, ‘journalists’ and politicians” of denying “that the English exist as a people”, a reference to Rees-Mogg’s description of the English as “a mongrel people”.

That, it said, was “genocidal rhetoric”, and it cited Gregory Stanton’s Ten Stages of Genocide, quoting a sentence about denying a group’s identity as a mechanism for mass crimes. But that sentence does not appear in Stanton’s model as published by Genocide Watch.

Stanton’s denial stage concerns perpetrators covering up a genocide: digging up mass graves, intimidating witnesses, blocking investigations. Rees-Mogg, for his part, had not denied that the English exist. He urged newcomers to “glory in the name of Englishman”.

What Stanton’s model does describe, in its fourth stage, is dehumanisation: members of a group “equated with animals, vermin, insects or diseases”. A day after invoking it, the Fellowship compared migrants to an infestation of invasive species.

Schools.

On 1 October, reacting to unrest in French schools, it wrote: “This is what happens when you try to assimilate the unassimilable.” It said parents should be free to choose “who their child goes to school with”.

A week later it announced it was preparing a homeschooling curriculum, beginning with “proper British history, taught clearly and without apology”. It cited, accurately, Department for Education figures showing 175,900 children in elective home education at some point in 2024/25.

Strength.

On 22 September it promised Fellows a nutrition and training plan, because “a people that cannot stand its ground will not keep its ground”. Boxing and martial arts, it said, build “the capacity to protect our families, communities, and our heritage”. @hopenothate has documented how far-right “Active Clubs” pair fitness with ideology. Fitness is not extremism. The framing is what deserves attention.

Asylum.

On 7 October its X account claimed that “over 93,000 migrants” were receiving government accommodation, 73,000 of them in “standard or HMO housing”, while NGOs helped “these people access luxuries we pay for”. 

The Fellowship, it said, exists for “securing a future for our people”, and would become “the only NGO to give our people a step up on the ladder we built”.

The figures don’t hold up. The 93,293 people the Home Office recorded as receiving asylum support at the end of June 2026 were asylum seekers, not migrants in general. That total includes 4,204 people receiving cash support only, with no accommodation. The 73,068 in non-hotel accommodation include initial and contingency sites as well as dispersal housing.

The post left out that the number receiving support had fallen 12% in a year, and that hotel use had halved.

Charity.

On 29 September, responding to a scheme letting charities sponsor refugees, it inverted the proverb: “They believe charity ends at home… For us, this is where charity begins.” The academic literature on movements like CasaPound has a term for this: welfare chauvinism, meaning support reserved for the in-group.

Self-determination.

On 9 October, responding to what a bookshop owner and an online activist each said were police visits to their homes, the Fellowship called for communities “cohesive enough to police themselves by shared standards”. It said that policing opinions “leaves us with no option but to find self-determination on our own terms”.

“Self-determination” is the vocabulary of peoples and nations, and “on our own terms” places it outside existing institutions. What it would mean in practice, the Fellowship does not say.

Not all of its output is hostile. One October post sets out how property wealth is concentrated among the over-60s, and how young people rent, delay starting families and are told to “wait for a will”. Its headline figures match Savills research published in March 2026, which found that over-60s hold 55% of Britain’s net housing wealth. Many economists would recognise the problem. But even there, the frame is a people’s survival: one that resents its young is “bound for self-destruction”, and one that supports them will “survive and thrive”.

The grievances are often real. What the Fellowship adds is the claim that they are, at root, about the survival of “our people”. Sellner’s own movement once published a manual on exactly this method: begin with widely shared grievances, then introduce the ideology gradually.

The Fellowship’s chosen launchpad was more explicit still. In the Lotus Eaters segment the Fellowship pinned to its profile, the presenter said that without electoral victory, projects like this will be swept away by legislation “once we become a minority”, and that they will not “outlive the replacement”.

“The replacement” is shorthand for the Great Replacement conspiracy theory. That theory claims white European populations are being deliberately replaced, and it has been cited by the perpetrators of mass-casualty attacks.

Another host praised organising that avoids “sticking bright flashing lights on itself” as a dissident movement. 

Organising quietly, without drawing attention, is precisely why this kind of early scrutiny matters.

These were the hosts’ words, and thanking a channel for promotion does not mean endorsing every remark. But the gap between the hosts’ language and the Fellowship’s is narrow.

An organisation that describes Britain as under “a hostile force of occupation”, ranks English “genetic continuity” against African and Asian populations, and compares migrants to invasive species is working within the same family of ideas.

We have seen this model before. Community provision as a route to influence is one of the best-documented strategies of the European far right.

Golden Dawn (Greece).

In 2012, members handed out food parcels outside the Greek parliament to people who could show ID proving Greek citizenship. When the Athens mayor banned later handouts, more than 2,000 people queued at the party’s headquarters instead. An Athens councillor quoted by AP summed it up: “At night they beat people up. And by day, they hand out food.”

CasaPound (Italy).

The movement grew from a housing occupation in Rome into a network running housing programmes, free legal advice and youth clubs. In their 2020 study, Froio, Castelli Gattinara, Bulli and Albanese argue that blending party and social-movement methods helped this fringe group consolidate its position and make extreme-right ideas routine in public debate.

Patriotic Alternative (UK).

Hope not Hate has documented how PA paired provocative stunts with a “family friendly” image of bake sales, hikes and litter picks. It also documented how PA and its offshoots tried to co-opt community campaigns, especially around asylum accommodation. Catherine Tebaldi and Alfonso Del Percio have shown how PA built community by branding and selling it. Membership tiers, pins, merchandise and a Round Table would be familiar to them.

The British scene is also reorganising. In August, Hope not Hate reported that PA is in decline, with former activists moving to Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain and to harder-line networks such as Active Clubs. Space is opening for new vehicles.

The differences matter too. Golden Dawn, founded as a neo-Nazi group, was ruled a criminal organisation by an Athens court in October 2020. PA is openly neo-Nazi. Nothing I have found shows the Wyvern Fellowship advocating violence or turning anyone away. The point is narrower and better documented: this organisational form, mutual aid and heritage and skills built around a paid membership, has repeatedly been used to build parallel institutions and make ethno-nationalist politics feel ordinary.

That history is a reason to watch closely; it is not yet evidence of where this group will go. Anyone who has studied moral panics knows the danger of inflating a small group into a looming menace. Overreaction plays into its hands. The Wyvern Fellowship was incorporated on 4 September 2026, is controlled by one man, and its Facebook page had 90 followers on 13 October. If First Ticket gets a handful of young people into work, that will be a good thing.

However, early warnings are most useful when they are actually early. In its first five weeks, the Fellowship has published six members-only essays and a steady stream of posts. What it has said in its own name imho already justifies attention:

- a “not for profit NGO” whose promises rest in documents its founder alone controls, with no accounts due until 2028;

- “support” that is so far mostly a subscription;

- “British communities” on one platform, “uniting patriots” on another, and “led by and for the British” on a third;

- migrants compared to invasive species, a lifeboat charity cast as the enemy, Britain described as under “a hostile force of occupation”, and a call for “self-determination on our own terms”;

- a launch on a platform whose hosts framed the project in Great Replacement terms, which the Fellowship pinned to the top of its profile.

Several things will show which way it goes:

- what its members-only essays and Discord contain;

- what its homeschooling curriculum teaches;

- whether its promised training plan stays a matter of fitness;

- who its First Ticket partners and “pro-British” employers turn out to be;

- whether it publishes and protects its asset lock;

- whether its services, as its own objects promise, stay “within safeguarding and equality law”;

- whether future chapters stay focused on skills and heritage or begin to appear around asylum accommodation. Given the Fellowship’s focus on asylum housing, how its housing-association guide gets used is worth watching.

“First Ticket” is a good name for a training scheme. It could also describe how far-right recruitment has often begun in the movements described above: the first ticket is the cheapest and it comes with something genuinely useful, but the final destination is rarely printed on it. The Wyvern Fellowship’s own words suggest where this line might run.  That’s reason enough to look closely now, while it is still at the first stop.

NOTES

Quotations from The Podcast of the Lotus Eaters #1515 (28 September 2026), Wyvern Fellowship segment, transcribed by the author. All other quotations are from material the Wyvern Fellowship has published openly on its website, X , or Facebook, accessed 13 October 2026. Sources consulted are in the next tweet.
